newsitem.title: YUGOSLAVIA: Serbian inquiry questions election annulments.
newsitem.headline: Serbian inquiry questions election annulments.

text.p: The Serbian government said on Tuesday a Justice Ministry inquiry found no fraud in a number of local elections annulled for that very reason, a disclosure that may have boosted the position of opposition protesters.

The announcement appeared at first glance to undercut the Socialist Party's' case for having nullified the elections, which a separate OSCE investigation determined had been won by the opposition Zajedno (Together) coalition.
Zajedno has staged nine straight weeks of street protests in a bid to have the election outcome reinstated and start Serbia on a long path to democratisation.

But the SPS-influenced Supreme Court has ruled since Monday that President Slobodan Milosevic's party won at least two of the towns in dispute and a lower court suspended a decision awarding Belgrade to Zajedno.

Uncertainty reigned after the Justice Ministry and Supreme Court announcements as to whether government hardliners bent on vanquishing Zajedno by any means or moderates willing to concede opposition victories were gaining the upper hand.

The initial reaction was confusion, something Western diplomats say has been deliberate Milosevic policy from the outset of the crisis as he seeks to avoid a handover of towns to Zajedno and avert renewed Western sanctions.

While granting that there were no irregularities in eight of 14 towns in dispute, the government made no mention of the annulment and did not say whether cancelling the outcome had been justified in the end.

"The Justice Ministry did not assess whether the objections and complaints to the decisions issued by these organs were justified because only courts are competent to do so," said a government statement issued by the official news agency Tanjug.
A municipal court confirmed a Zajedno victory in Serbia's second city Nis, a week ago and threw out an SPS appeal.
But other courts have dealt blows to Zajedno's campaign.

The municipal court in Belgrade, grand prize in the Serbia-wide regional elections and not one of the eight towns cited by the ministry, suspended an electoral commission ruling last week that Zajedno had won the capital.
And the Supreme Court has ruled the SPS took the towns of Smederevska Palanka and Sabac, both on the list of eight said by the Justice Ministry to have enjoyed clean elections.
The Organisation for Security and Cooperation in Europe upheld Zajedno's claim to have been robbed of victory in all 14 disputed towns by a fraudulent decision to annul the outcome.
Two prominent opposition officials were divided as to the meaning of the government announcement, with one saying it vindicated Zajedno and the other dismissing it as obfuscation.
"In this statement the government has in the clearest terms said that the Zajedno coalition absolutely won in those eight municipalties," said Goran Draganic, a Zajedno lawyer.

Asked why the announcement made no mention of Belgrade or Nis, Draganic said Serbian authorities were "leaving the best for the last trade-off. But they are mistaken in believing wre will compromise on any single seat we won in the elections".
Milan Bozic, political adviser to Zajedno co-leader Vuk Draskovic, said that the government had in fact rejected the OSCE report and described its statement as a play to buy time.
Earlier, informed sources said Milosevic was considering a plan to defuse the protests by imposing provisional rule in Belgrade for two months and then calling a new vote.

Under current law, provisional government can be declared in a town if its assembly has not been convened within 60 days of an election -- the case in Belgrade. But new elections should be called two months later.
It was not clear whether this strategy might be expanded to cover other contested cities.

The political sources, close to Milosevic's secretive inner circle, stressed this was only one of several options proposed in an unresolved internal debate and conceded it would almost certainly not placate opposition protesters.

An opposition takeover at municipal level would start democratic reform in Serbian-led federal Yugoslavia, under communist/socialist rule since World War Two, by breaking leftist strangleholds on the main media and judiciary.

Some 50,000 Zajedno faithful rallied in Belgrade on Tuesday, the 65th day of protests across Serbia. A planned taxi blockade of Belgrade bridges did not transpire after the police reportedly started confiscating cabbies' driving licences .
